scenarios.title: What if the Bronze Age Collapse hadn't happened?
scenarios.summary: A counterfactual in which the Late Bronze Age palatial systems of the eastern Mediterranean survive the c. 1200 BCE crisis, letting the Hittite, Mycenaean and Ugaritic networks continue.

overlays.label: Hittite Empire persists
overlays.note: Central Anatolia remains a unified Hittite state rather than fragmenting into Neo-Hittite city-states.

overlays.label: Mycenaean palaces endure
overlays.note: The Aegean palatial economy survives instead of giving way to the Greek Dark Age.

overlays.label: Tin trade route continues
overlays.note: Long-distance tin exchange from the east keeps supplying Mediterranean bronze workshops.

overlays.label: Ugarit survives
overlays.note: The cosmopolitan port of Ugarit is never destroyed and remains a hub of alphabetic literacy.

sources: Cline, E. H. (2014). 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed.
Speculative educational overlay — not a scholarly reconstruction.

scenarios.title: What if the Indo-European expansion had stalled?
scenarios.summary: A counterfactual in which steppe pastoralist expansions do not spread Indo-European languages across Europe and South Asia, leaving pre-existing language families dominant.

overlays.label: Pre-Indo-European Europe endures
overlays.note: Neolithic 'Old European' language families persist across the continent instead of being replaced.

overlays.label: Dravidian languages remain across South Asia
overlays.note: Without Indo-Aryan migration, Dravidian and other pre-existing families cover the whole subcontinent.

sources: Anthony, D. W. (2007). The Horse, the Wheel, and Language.
Speculative educational overlay — not a scholarly reconstruction.
